title: Getting things done
grammar: The causative: have / get something done

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Back to the workshop! This time you'll learn to talk about jobs you arrange for other people — the causative — and how to describe things that need fixing.
scene.intro: Welcome back to Unit 2. The Inspiring Nordic project returns to the workshop, but this time we look at who actually does the work. You will read a project diary in the format of Reading and Use of English Part 6 (gapped text), listen to eight short conversations about services and repairs in the format of Listening Part 1, learn the causative — have and get something done — for talking about jobs we arrange for other people, and a second language focus on describing problems and reporting faults. By the end of the unit you will be able to write a clear, polite email explaining exactly what went wrong and what should be done about it. Let's get things done.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (about 2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves in turn — home, studies, free time, likes and dislikes. Part 2 (about 4 minutes in total): you look at three photographs and talk on your own for about a minute, comparing two of them and answering the question printed above them; then your partner answers a short question about your photographs (about 30 seconds).
how: In Part 1, answer with a reason or a short example — a single word or a memorised sentence loses marks.
In Part 2, don't just describe the photographs one by one: compare them, and make sure you answer both parts of the question above them.
Use modals of speculation when you're not sure — might, could, may, possibly — rather than stating guesses as facts.
Keep talking for the full minute; if you run out of things to say about one photo, move to the question again.
tips.remember: Fluency matters more than perfect grammar here — stopping to correct every small mistake costs you more marks than the mistake itself.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 6 — gapped text. Choose the paragraph that fits each gap.

tips.expect: Reading and Use of English Part 6: one text of 500–650 words with six paragraphs removed and placed, in a different order, after the text, together with one extra paragraph that does not fit anywhere. You decide which paragraph fits each of the six gaps.
how: Read the base text first, ignoring the gaps, to understand the overall story or argument.
Look for links just before and after each gap: pronouns (it, this, they), time expressions (by half term, that was only the beginning), and topic words that must match what comes next.
Check your choice by reading the gap together with the sentences BEFORE and AFTER it — a paragraph that fits grammatically may still break the flow of ideas.
tips.remember: One paragraph is a distractor and will not be used. If you have used the same letter twice, at least one of your answers must be wrong.

data.title: How we built our workshop, one phone call at a time
data.text:
When our class agreed to turn an unused storeroom into a proper woodworking workshop for the Inspiring Nordic project, none of us expected how many phone calls it would take. We had plenty of ideas and almost no practical skills, so from the very first week we learned to rely on other people's trades rather than our own.

{1}

That was only the beginning.

{2}

Meanwhile, not every job needed an outside expert.

{3}

The trickiest call, by far, concerned the wiring.

{4}

By half term, the room finally looked like a workshop rather than a storeroom.

{5}

Even so, a few things still needed attention.

{6}

Looking back, the workshop taught us something the timetable never could: that getting a job done well usually means knowing who to ask, not how to do it yourself.

paragraphs.text: With solid walls at last, we turned our attention to furniture. None of us could build a proper workbench, so we asked a carpenter in town for a quotation. A week later we had six sturdy benches made from recycled timber, delivered on a trailer. Mateo says the smell of fresh sawdust is his favourite memory of the whole project.

Getting the electrics checked was far more serious. An old socket had been sparking for years, and nobody in our class was foolish enough to touch it. We had a qualified electrician inspect the whole room, and he insisted on replacing the wiring completely before any machinery could be plugged in. Safety, he told us, is never a job worth doing yourself.

One problem only appeared once the room was in daily use: a tap in the corner sink kept dripping. We reported the fault to the school caretaker, who agreed that it needed fixing rather than ignoring, and a plumber sorted it out within the week. It was a small job, but it taught us that even a finished project needs looking after.

A local mason came round on the very first Saturday. The old storeroom walls were cracked and damp in places, so we had them repaired and replastered before we could do anything else. It took him two days, and he charged less than we had feared once he saw how small the room was. Sofía kept a photo diary of the work, which later became part of our project report.

For the summer fair, the school also decided to hire a caterer instead of running the usual cake stall. A local company was commissioned to bring a small van and serve hot food to visiting families. It proved so popular that teachers are already asking whether it should become a yearly tradition rather than a one-off treat.

Painting the shelves, however, was something we could manage without professional help. Liam and Nadia spent an entire Wednesday afternoon sanding and repainting the old shelving units a cheerful blue, and Miss Vega let us skip half of double Maths to finish the job. It was hard work, but at least it didn't cost the project a penny.

The final touch was the sign above the door. Nadia designed a logo on her tablet, and we had it engraved on a sheet of metal by a signwriter who usually works for local shops. By half term it was fixed proudly to the wall, and visitors finally knew, without asking, what the room was for.

activities.title: Language focus 1 — the causative: have/get something done

data.title: The causative: have/get something done (and have someone do something)
data.can: I can use have/get + object + past participle to talk about work I arrange for someone else, and have + person + base form to say exactly who does it.
data.intro: In this unit's reading, the students didn't do most of the work themselves — they arranged for other people to do it. English has two related structures for this: have/get something done, when we focus on the job, and have someone do something, when we focus on the person who does it.

examples.text: We had the walls repaired by a local mason.
examples.note: have + object + past participle = we arranged it, we didn't do it

examples.text: We're getting the electrics checked this week.
examples.note: get is a little more informal than have

examples.text: We had an electrician inspect the whole room.
examples.note: have + person + base form (no 'to') = names who does the job

examples.text: Can you get the carpenter to deliver the benches on Friday?
examples.note: get + person + to + infinitive = informal version of 'have someone do'
an everyday, personal example — not always about tradespeople

rules: Have/get + object + past participle: someone else does the action FOR us. Focus is on the result: We had the sign made.
Have + person + base form (no 'to'): names WHO does it. It sounds a little more like an instruction: We had an electrician inspect the wiring.
Get + person + to + infinitive is the informal equivalent of 'have + person + base form': We got the electrician to inspect the wiring.
Do NOT say 'get someone do something' — with get, the infinitive needs 'to'.
Get (rather than have) is usual when the job needs some persuading or arranging: Can you get him to hurry up?

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

tips.expect: Reading and Use of English Part 2: a short text of 150–200 words with eight gaps. You write ONE word in each gap — no options are given. Most answers are grammatical words: prepositions, articles, pronouns, auxiliaries, conjunctions and relative words.
how: Read the whole text first before filling any gap — later sentences often make an earlier gap obvious.
Look at the words immediately before and after the gap: does a verb need a particular preposition? Does a clause need a relative pronoun?
Write only one word per gap, and check your spelling carefully.
tips.remember: Contractions are not accepted, and a correct word spelt wrongly scores nothing.

data.text: Before you have any work done on your home, it pays to plan carefully. First, ask {1} least three tradespeople for a quotation, {2} that you can compare prices fairly. Never assume that the cheapest quote is the best value: a professional {3} charges slightly more may finish the job faster and to a higher standard. Once you have chosen someone, ask for references from previous customers and, {4} possible, look at photographs of finished work. A trusted recommendation can save you both time and money. {5} soon as the job begins, keep a written record of {6} was agreed, including dates and costs, so that any disagreement can be settled quickly. Good communication protects both sides: the customer gets the work {7} wanted, and the tradesperson is paid on time and without argument. Finally, remember that a fair price does not always mean the lowest one. It is often worth paying a little more for craftsmanship that will last for years rather {8} having the same job done twice.

activities.title: Listening Part 1 — eight short extracts. Choose the best answer for each.

tips.expect: Listening Part 1: eight short, unrelated extracts (monologues or conversations between two speakers). For each one you answer a single three-option multiple-choice question about gist, detail, function, opinion or attitude. You hear each extract twice.
how: Before each extract plays, read its question and three options quickly so you know exactly what to listen for.
The correct answer is often a paraphrase of what you hear, not the exact words — be careful of an option that repeats a word from the recording but changes its meaning.
If you are not sure after the first listening, choose your best guess and use the second listening to confirm or change it.
tips.remember: Never leave an answer blank — an educated guess has a one-in-three chance; a blank has none.

data.voice_note: Varias voces distintas (hombres y mujeres) en ocho extractos breves e independientes: conversaciones, un mensaje de voz y un anuncio, todos sobre encargar y hablar de trabajos y servicios.
data.script:
Extract 1:
Woman: You still riding that bike with the wobbly wheel, or did you finally get it looked at?
Man: I took it to the shop on the corner last week, actually. They said the wheel wasn't even worth repairing — I'd be better off getting a new one.
Woman: So what did you do?
Man: I had them fit a secondhand wheel instead. Cost me almost nothing, and honestly, it rides better now than it ever did before.
Woman: Good for you — mine's been making a strange clicking noise for weeks.
[pause]
Extract 2:
Claire: Hi, it's Claire Dunmore here, from Flat 3. I left a message on Monday about the leak under the kitchen sink, but nobody's called back yet. It's getting worse, and I really need someone to come and have a look before the weekend, if that's at all possible. I'll be in most evenings after six, or you can try my mobile during the day. Please let me know when you can fit me in — thanks.
[pause]
Extract 3:
Announcer: Is your kitchen looking a little tired? At Hollis Decorating, we don't just paint walls — we transform rooms, and we always finish on the day we promise. Every job comes with a free, no-obligation quotation, and all our painters are fully insured and DBS-checked. Call us this month and get your hallway decorated absolutely free when you book any two other rooms. Hollis Decorating: getting it done properly, the first time.
[pause]
Extract 4:
Man: Have you seen the quote for repainting reception? It's almost double what we paid last time.
Woman: I know, but the company we used before went out of business, remember? This lot came highly recommended, though — Sam had his whole flat done by them.
Man: Fair enough. As long as they don't leave it looking like a building site for a fortnight, I'm not going to argue about the price.
Woman: Just don't let them start until after half term, whatever you do.
[pause]
Extract 5:
Customer: I brought my laptop in three weeks ago to have the screen replaced, and it's still not ready.
Assistant: I do apologise. Let me check... ah, I see the part that was ordered arrived damaged, so we had to send off for another one.
Customer: Nobody told me that. I've been calling every few days for an update.
Assistant: You're quite right, and I'm sorry. We'll also take ten per cent off the final bill for the inconvenience.
[pause]
Extract 6:
Teacher: Have the posters for the exhibition come back from the printers yet?
Student: Not yet, Miss. They said Thursday, but the sizes we asked for meant they had to order special paper first.
Teacher: As long as they're ready before Saturday morning, we'll be fine.
Student: That's what they promised. I rang this morning just to check, and they confirmed everything's on schedule.
Teacher: Good. Let the others know, so nobody panics if the posters aren't here by Friday.
[pause]
Extract 7:
Danny: Hello, this is Danny from Fenwick Building Services, returning your call about the garden wall. I've had a look at the photos you sent, and I reckon it's about a three-day job, materials included. I'll pop round on Thursday afternoon if that suits, just to measure up properly before I give you a final figure — the price I mentioned is only a rough estimate at this stage. Give me a ring if Thursday's no good.
[pause]
Extract 8:
Woman: You had your fence done in the end, then? It looks great.
Man: Thanks — we got a local carpenter to build it rather than buying one of those flat-pack ones. Took him longer than he'd said, mind you, nearly two weeks instead of five days.
Woman: Did he have to order any special wood for it?
Man: Just a bit, yes, which is partly why it took longer.
Woman: Still, good things come to those who wait, as they say.

activities.title: Language focus 2 — describing problems and services

data.title: Describing problems and services: needs + -ing, should have been done, reporting faults
data.can: I can say that something needs attention using needs/wants + -ing, criticise a past action with should/shouldn't have been done, and use the passive to report a fault.
data.intro: Once work has been arranged, we often need to describe what still needs doing, or complain politely about what should — or shouldn't — have happened. These structures are close cousins of the causative and are essential for writing about services and complaints.

examples.text: That tap needs fixing — it's been dripping for a week.
examples.note: needs + -ing = needs to be fixed (active form, passive meaning)

examples.text: This form needs to be signed before Friday.
examples.note: needs + to be + past participle = same meaning, more formal

examples.text: The wiring should have been checked years ago.
examples.note: should have been + past participle = criticising something that didn't happen but should have

examples.text: That shelf shouldn't have been painted before the plaster had dried.
examples.note: shouldn't have been + past participle = it happened, but it was wrong

examples.text: Any faults must be reported to the caretaker immediately.
examples.note: passive for official rules and procedures

rules: Needs/wants + verb-ing is an informal way of saying something needs to be done: The door needs painting.
Needs/wants + to be + past participle means exactly the same, and is a little more formal or explicit: The door needs to be painted.
Should/shouldn't + have been + past participle criticises a past action or a past omission — it did or didn't happen, and it was wrong.
Use the ordinary passive (is/was/has been + past participle) to describe official processes, rules or reporting faults, especially when who does it is unknown or unimportant.
These structures combine naturally with the causative: We had it fixed because it needed fixing.

Don't worry about the door — it only ___ a little oil on the hinges.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze. Choose the best word for each gap.

tips.expect: Reading and Use of English Part 1: a short text of 150–200 words with eight gaps, each followed by four options. The options are usually close in meaning, and you choose the one that fits the exact word or phrase used around the gap — often a collocation, a phrasal verb or a fixed expression.
how: Read the whole text first to understand the topic before choosing any answer.
For each gap, check which option forms a natural collocation or fixed phrase with the words around it — the other three often make sense in isolation but not in that exact combination.
If two options seem possible, check the grammar around the gap: does the verb need a preposition that only one option takes?
tips.remember: This part tests vocabulary, not grammar — all four options are usually the same part of speech.

data.title: Calling in the professionals
data.text: When something goes wrong at home, it is tempting to {1} the job yourself rather than pay a professional. Sometimes that saves money; more often, it ends up {2} more than it would have cost in the first place. Before you {3} a builder, decorator or electrician, it is worth asking friends and family for a personal {4}, since word of mouth is usually more reliable than an online review. A trusted recommendation can save you both time and money. Once you have a shortlist, {5} in touch with at least two tradespeople for a quotation. Never agree to anything on the {6} of a phone call alone. A good tradesperson will not mind you asking questions, and will happily {7} you through exactly what the job involves. Finally, resist the temptation to {8} the cheapest option without checking their previous work — a bargain price is no bargain at all if the job has to be done twice.

activities.title: Writing Part 2 — email. Plan, write 140–190 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Part 2 offers you a choice of tasks — an article, an email/letter or a review. An email or letter usually responds to a situation with notes or a previous message, and asks you to cover two or three specific points. 140–190 words, in a style appropriate to the person you are writing to.
how: Read the input carefully and note exactly which points you must cover — missing one loses marks even if your English is excellent.
Match your style to the person you are writing to: neutral or semi-formal for someone you don't know well, like a company manager.
Organise your email logically: one clear idea per paragraph, with a greeting and a suitable closing.
tips.remember: You are marked on content, communicative achievement, organisation and language — covering all the points matters as much as accurate grammar.

data.task:
You recently had some building work done at a community club where you help out, but there have been some problems. Read part of an email from Mr Hart, the manager of the company that did the work, and the notes you have made.

“…I understand there were some issues with the work our team carried out last week. Please let me know exactly what happened, and what you would like us to do about it, so we can put things right.”

  • which job wasn't finished properly
  • a problem that needs fixing urgently
  • what you want the company to do next

Write an email to Mr Hart. Write 140–190 words in an appropriate style.
plan: Opening: thank him for his email and say you will explain what happened.
Paragraph 2: name the job that wasn't finished properly, with one concrete detail.
Paragraph 3: describe the urgent problem clearly and why it matters.
Closing: say exactly what you want the company to do next, and end politely.

Opening and referring back: I am writing to explain exactly what happened.
Describing a problem: It clearly needs looking at as soon as possible.
Making a request: I would be grateful if you could...
What we would like is for someone to...
Closing: I look forward to hearing from you.
Please let me know as soon as possible.
Thank you for your help with this.

checklist: I have referred to Mr Hart's email at the start.
I have named the job that wasn't finished properly.
I have explained the urgent problem clearly.
I have said exactly what I want the company to do next.
The register is semi-formal throughout: no slang, but not stiffly formal either.
data.model:
A model answer (150 words).

Dear Mr Hart,

Thank you for getting in touch so quickly. I am happy to explain exactly what happened last week.

The main problem is that the shelving in the storeroom was never finished. Your team fitted two of the three units, but left before completing the last one, so we still cannot use that part of the room properly.

More urgently, one of the electrical sockets your electrician installed on Tuesday has started sparking whenever anyone switches it on. We have taped over it and stopped using it, but it clearly needs looking at as soon as possible, since children use the club every afternoon.

I would be grateful if you could send someone to finish the shelving and check the faulty socket this week, if at all possible. We would also appreciate written confirmation once both jobs have been completed.

Thank you for your help with this.

Best wishes,
Nadia

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 3 minutes): you and your partner discuss a question together, using five written prompts arranged around it, then spend about a minute reaching a decision. Part 4 (about 4 minutes): the examiner asks you both further, more general questions on the same topic.
how: In Part 3 you are marked on how well you interact, not on whether you agree — ask your partner's opinion, respond to it, and build on what they say.
Do not try to discuss all five prompts in detail; two or three explored properly is better than five rushed ones.
In the decision minute, negotiate rather than simply stating your own view: Shall we agree that...? I could go along with that, as long as...
In Part 4, develop each answer with a reason and an example, not just a one-line opinion.
tips.remember: You do not have to complete Part 3's discussion of all five prompts, and you are not marked on whether you and your partner agree — only on how well you interact.
